classification_signals: Abstract mentions 'evidence in support of a new configurational paradigm' and 'configurational correlates of movement patterns'.
Introduction discusses 'quantitative methods for predicting pedestrian movement'.
Section 'Case study 1: King's Cross' (p. 36) details an 'extensive firsthand investigation of space use and movement' with 'observation technique'.
The paper presents 'scattergrams' and 'correlation coefficients' (e.g., Figures 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, Tables 1, 2, 3) from observed data.
It includes 'axial maps' (e.g., Figures 8, 21, 27) and 'black-on-white space maps' (e.g., Figures 20, 26) as analytical tools.
The paper explicitly states 'Our aim in this paper is to set out the evidence for natural movement...' (p. 33).
It describes 'space syntax' as a 'new technique of configurational analysis' and its application to 'observing space use and movement' (p. 32).
The 'Implication for theory' section (p. 62) discusses theoretical consequences derived from the empirical findings.

limitations: It is difficult to show unambiguously and numerically how a major interruption of route continuity and destination availability (King's Cross site as a 'negative attractor') has local 'negative multiplier' effects on the surrounding area (p. 50).
Much further research is needed in the area of 'negative attractors' (p. 50).
Current database and software do not permit excising areas from a larger system to compute mean integration values read within the large system for comparison with mean encounter rates (p. 48).
It is not possible to take the ten routes as fully representative of their well-defined areas (p. 48).

The City case study's differences between local subareas may be due to differential distribution of built forms or the regional character of the City grid, requiring further research to clarify (p. 56).
The contextual area for the Krüger study (Brazilian towns) was insufficient to give an adequate syntactic picture of the study area (p. 61).
Much remains to be understood about the 'ceteris paribus' clause in the theory of natural movement (p. 61).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study proposes a 'configurational' paradigm for urban pedestrian movement, arguing that the urban grid's configuration, particularly its 'integration' (a global space syntax measure), is the primary generator of movement patterns, with attractors acting as multipliers. Case studies in King's Cross, the City of London, and a South London housing estate demonstrate strong correlations between integration and movement rates, often logarithmic when attractors are present, and linear when they are excluded. The paper highlights that local spatial properties are less important than global configurational relations for predicting movement, and that modern housing estates often suffer from 'underscaling' leading to peripheralized movement and isolation. Limitations include difficulties in isolating attractor effects from configurational ones with current tools and the need for further research into 'negative attractors' and the 'ceteris paribus' clause.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The spatial configuration of urban street networks is a primary determinant of pedestrian movement patterns, often referred to as 'natural movement'.
Human movement and spatial behavior are significantly influenced by the underlying topological and geometric properties of space.

mechanism_chain.description: The spatial configuration of the urban grid influences how easily people can perceive and navigate the space, which in turn shapes their route choices and overall pedestrian movement patterns.
